screeningScope: Full-text source, eligibility, taxonomy, and synthesis-readiness review of current shortlist positions 1-6.

decisionDefinitions.INCLUDE: Eligible for evidence extraction and synthesis after full-text review.
decisionDefinitions.DEGRADED: A required source or verification element was unavailable.

records.sourceFile: The acute effects of twenty four hours of sleep loss on the performance of national caliber male collegiate weightlifters.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: The local PDF omits the DOI; PubMed PMID 18076267 confirms this DOI and source identity.

records.evidenceSummary: In a randomized counterbalanced crossover, nine national-caliber male collegiate weightlifters completed maximal snatch, clean-and-jerk, and front-squat sessions after 24 hours awake and after normal sleep. Measured lifting volume and intensity did not differ significantly, while mood disturbance and sleepiness worsened after sleep loss.
records.limitations: Only nine men and one acute total-sleep-loss exposure were studied. A nonsignificant performance difference does not establish equivalence or safety, and this design does not address chronic restriction, team-sport play, or injury risk.
records.synthesisCaution: Do not present one preserved weightlifting session as evidence that sleep loss is harmless. Treat sleepiness and altered mood as relevant staff signals, and protect adequate sleep opportunity.

records.sourceFile: The Dark Side of College Football.pdf
records.exclusionReason: This two-page Sports Health editorial discusses safety concerns and cites other studies but does not report original methods or a systematic evidence synthesis. Its numerical claims require the cited primary sources before publication as evidence.

records.sourceFile: To train or not to train (on match day) - Influence of a priming session on match performance in competitive elite-level soccer.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Across 32 elite-soccer matches, the club's matches preceded by a 15-20-minute morning priming session had greater total, moderate-speed, and high-speed running distance than matches without it; technical measures were generally similar.
records.limitations: The comparison was observational within one club, primed and unprimed match observations were unequal, and the specific routine and player context limit transfer. Residual match and selection confounding prevents a causal efficacy claim.
records.synthesisCaution: A brief morning routine is a candidate to test in local match preparation, not an established requirement or proof that priming itself improved match performance.

records.sourceFile: Training load and injury risk in elite Rugby Union - The largest investigation to date.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Two-season data from 696 professional rugby players, 13 clubs, and 1,718 all-type injuries compared multiple acute:chronic workload-ratio calculations. Significant associations varied markedly by calculation; no method consistently related ratio to injury.
records.limitations: The observational analysis cannot establish causation or prevention. Load was represented by session-RPE, injury definitions and model choices matter, and the rugby setting does not provide a universal threshold for other sports.
records.synthesisCaution: Do not use an ACWR sweet spot or a single ratio as an injury-risk rule. Review load progression alongside symptoms, exposure, context, and clinical judgment.

records.sourceFile: Weekly external load performance effects on sports injuries of male professional soccer players.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: In one season of 33 male professional soccer players, 15 sustained 24 recorded injuries. Four-week pre-injury blocks had higher total distance, high-speed running, accelerations, and decelerations than four-week post-return blocks and player season averages.
records.limitations: One team, one season, 24 injuries, pandemic-period conditions, and comparisons with post-injury return make the direction of causation uncertain. Match context, exposure, and injury severity were not adequately resolved for an individual risk threshold.
records.synthesisCaution: Use the findings to prompt contextual load review, not to label a GPS spike as a validated injury predictor or prescribe a fixed ceiling.

records.sourceFile: Weekly programming of hamstring-related training contents in European professional soccer.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: A cross-sectional questionnaire of European professional soccer strength and conditioning coaches described where hamstring-demanding exercises and high-speed exposures are placed in a match-week microcycle. Respondents commonly reported heavier hamstring work around match day minus four or three and lighter work near matches.
records.limitations: Self-reported practice patterns are not tests of injury prevention or performance. Competition representation varied, England and Germany were absent, and team injury outcomes were not collected.
records.synthesisCaution: Treat the reported microcycle as a map of practice, not an evidence-based timetable or an injury-prevention effect. Adapt loading to match schedule, athlete capacity, and local outcomes.
